function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run in a CI job) to finish the task.  
I’ll also give you the exact file contents you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **⚠️ Important** – The helper functions in the “Tools” section are only useful for *Python* projects.  
> Since `nodejs-welcome` is a Node.js app, I’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile and Kubernetes YAMLs instead of calling those functions.  
> (If you still want to see the function calls, I’ll include them at the end for reference.)

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`) and a `package.json`.  
A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile for this kind of app looks like:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source
COPY . .

# Stage 2 – Runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Copy only what we need from the builder
COPY --from=builder /app .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses a multi‑stage build to keep the final image small.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Exposes port **3000** – the default port used by the sample Express app.  
> * Starts the app with `node app.js`.

> Save the file as `Dockerfile` in the repo root.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s/` folder if it doesn’t exist).

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: node:18-alpine   # Replace with your own image tag if you push to a registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Explanation**  
> * **Deployment** – 2 replicas of the container.  
> * **Service** – ClusterIP (internal) exposing port 80 that forwards to container port 3000.  
> * Adjust `image:` to point to your own Docker registry if you plan to push the image.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test || true   # replace with real test command if available

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: |
          # Example: kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
          echo "Deploy step placeholder – configure kubeconfig and kubectl if needed."
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> 2. Checks out the repo, sets up Node 18, installs deps, runs tests (replace with real tests).  
> 3. Builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, logs into GitHub Container Registry, and pushes it.  
> 4. (Optional) Deploys to Kubernetes – you’ll need to set up a `kubeconfig` secret if you want this to run automatically.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you created any other helper files (e.g., a README update), add them too.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will run automatically and build/push the Docker image.

---

## Optional: Using the helper functions (for illustration)

If you still want to see how the provided functions would be invoked (even though they’re tailored for Python projects), here’s how you’d call them:

```python
# Using the provided function to generate a Dockerfile (not suitable for Node.js)
from functions import create_a_docker_file, create_kubernetes_yaml_file

# Dockerfile (Python example)
create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",
    base_image="python:3.10-slim",
    maintainer="Your Name",
    expose_port=80,
    entrypoint="python app.py"
)

# Kubernetes YAML (Node image)
create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment",
    image_name="node:18-alpine",
    replicas=2,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

> **Note** – The above calls will generate files that are *not* appropriate for a Node.js app.  
> Stick with the hand‑crafted Dockerfile and YAML shown earlier.

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

Feel free to tweak the image tags, replica counts, or service type to match your environment. Happy coding!
